name: Pioneer 11
significance: Pioneer 11 followed Pioneer 10 through the asteroid belt and then went much closer to Jupiter, passing 42,500 km above the cloud tops in December 1974, three times closer than its twin, and taking the first pictures of Jupiter's polar regions. Its high speed carried it through the intense radiation belts quickly enough to survive. Jupiter's gravity then swung it back across the Solar System to Saturn, and on 1 September 1979 it became the first spacecraft to visit Saturn. It found the first conclusive evidence of Saturn's magnetic field, discovered a new narrow ring outside the known rings (the F ring) and a small new moon, saw Titan as a featureless orange ball at about -193 C, and found Saturn to be mostly liquid hydrogen. It then headed out of the Solar System toward the centre of the galaxy, carrying the same gold plaque as Pioneer 10.
statusNote: Launched 1973-04-06 02:11 UTC (5 April EST, the date on NASA's launch photo) on an Atlas-Centaur from Cape Kennedy (Horizons; Siddiqi, Beyond Earth). Passed through the asteroid belt by mid-March 1974. Jupiter closest approach 1974-12-03 05:22 UT at 42,500 km above the cloud tops (Siddiqi; Horizons' header says 42,000 km, NASA's 1995 release 26,600 miles); Horizons puts it at 05:21, 113,518 km from Jupiter's centre. Saturn: bow shock 1979-08-31, ring-plane crossing 14:36 UT and closest approach 16:31 UT on 1979-09-01 at 20,900 km (Siddiqi; Horizons' header says within 21,000 km of the cloud tops; Horizons puts it at 16:30, 80,862 km from Saturn's centre). Crossed Neptune's orbit 1990-02-23 (Siddiqi). NASA ended daily communications on 1995-09-30, when its power was too low to run the instruments, 44.1 AU from Earth (NASA release 95-163; Siddiqi); a few minutes of engineering data came on 1995-11-24 (Siddiqi). TRAJECTORY: JPL Horizons -24, "provided by JPL Navigation Team" from source files PN11A-G and DE118; Horizons notes the regeneration of those files "is not well known" and that the trajectory suits "general historical purposes". Drawn solid from Horizons to the last contact, 1995-09-30; after that Horizons' path is a projection with no tracking behind it, so it is drawn dashed out to 54.514 AU from the Sun (1.1 x Pluto's farthest distance), where it leaves the Solar System view and continues in the heliosphere view. Jupiter and Saturn tours in the planet views (tools/build_voyager.py, tools/build_planet_tour.py). Moon distances: closest approaches computed from Horizons (tools/moon_passes.py).

legs._comment: Heliocentric path built 2026-11-27 by tools/build_voyager.py from JPL Horizons (target -24): Lambert legs between real positions; planet tours spliced in; ends where the craft passes 54.514 AU (1.1 x Pluto's aphelion), the edge of the Solar System view for now.

Jupiter tour built 2026-11-27 by tools/build_planet_tour.py from JPL Horizons (target -24, 1974-11-30 -> 1974-12-06): one planetocentric Lambert arc per piece between real periapses, moon flybys (pinned to the moon's modeled position) and filler waypoints keeping each piece under 60 deg / 1 d.

Saturn tour built 2026-11-27 by tools/build_planet_tour.py from JPL Horizons (target -24, 1979-08-29 -> 1979-09-04): one planetocentric Lambert arc per piece between real periapses, moon flybys (pinned to the moon's modeled position) and filler waypoints keeping each piece under 60 deg / 1 d.
Contact ended 1995-09-30: from here the path is Horizons' projection with no tracking behind it, drawn dashed.
2000-01-07T13:00:00Z: crosses 54.514 AU from the Sun (Horizons, hourly); the Solar System view stops the path here, and the heliosphere layer carries it on.

heliospherePath.note: Heliocentric ecliptic J2000 positions from JPL Horizons every 60 days. Solid to 1995-09-30, dashed after: the rest is Horizons' prediction, a projection. Past the Solar System view's edge (54.514 AU) from 2000-01-07. NASA ended contact on 1995-09-30, before then, so this whole stretch is a projection of Horizons' trajectory and is drawn dashed.
